controversies/mysticism-and-orthodoxy/qu: When does the pursuit of union with God become heresy?
controversies/mysticism-and-orthodoxy/ti: Mysticism and orthodoxy: Eckhart, the hesychasts and the quietists
controversies/mysticism-and-orthodoxy/su: Mystics claim direct experience of God beyond words; church authorities must judge whether such claims fit the faith. The East vindicated the hesychasts (1341-51), while the West condemned propositions of Meister Eckhart (1329), and later Molinos (1687) and Fénelon (1699), even as it canonised Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross. Protestants were divided between admiration and suspicion. The cases show how traditions test mystical claims.
controversies/mysticism-and-orthodoxy/si: God is greater than every concept, so the soul must let go of images and self-will to find God in its depths. Paradoxical language is the only honest way to speak of union with the infinite. Our teaching aims at humility and love, and we submit it to the Church’s judgement; the condemnations seized on phrases torn from context.
Language implies identity of soul and God

The Church honours true mystics, but must protect the faithful from teachings that blur the Creator-creature distinction, make the sacraments and moral struggle unnecessary, or encourage passivity toward sin. Experience must be judged by the faith handed down, and pastors must guard simple believers from misunderstandings that popular preaching can spread.
Condemnations sometimes motivated by politics and misreadings

There is no opposition between dogma and mysticism: theology is the experience of the saints, and the councils that upheld Palamas showed that the Church can recognise genuine vision of the uncreated light while rejecting rationalist objections.
Western critics of the essence-energies distinction

God does not wait for us at the top of a ladder of ascent; he comes down to us in Christ, the Word preached and the sacraments. Mystical claims to immediate union bypass the one Mediator and the external Word, and enthusiasts who trust inner voices end in confusion.
Scripture speaks of union and vision
controversies/mysticism-and-orthodoxy/ti: Marguerite Porete burned in Paris for The Mirror of Simple Souls.
In agro dominico condemns 28 propositions from Eckhart.
Constantinople council upholds Palamas against Barlaam.
Spanish Index bans many vernacular spiritual books; Teresa’s writings later examined by the Inquisition.

Pius XI declares John of the Cross a Doctor of the Church.
Teresa of Ávila becomes the first woman Doctor of the Church.
controversies/mysticism-and-orthodoxy/re: Orthodoxy made hesychast mysticism part of its dogmatic identity. Catholicism canonised some mystics and condemned others, and modern scholarship has rehabilitated Eckhart’s reputation without formal revocation of the bull. Protestants remain divided between appreciation and suspicion of mysticism.
controversies/mysticism-and-orthodoxy/co: Caution about vernacular mysticism in the late medieval and early modern West.
Distinctive Orthodox fusion of mysticism and doctrine.
Protestant readers adopted condemned Catholic mystics (Guyon, Molinos) in Pietist and Holiness circles.
controversies/faith-and-reason-via-antiq: Can reason prove what faith believes, or must faith stand on revelation alone?
Faith and reason: via antiqua versus via moderna

Medieval theologians agreed that faith and reason come from the same God, but disagreed about how far reason reaches. The realist "via antiqua" of Thomists (and Scotists) held that reason can demonstrate God’s existence and grasp real natures; the nominalist "via moderna" of Ockham and Biel limited demonstration and grounded the order of salvation in God’s free covenant. The debate shaped the Reformation, the Catholic revival of Thomism and modern disputes about natural theology.
Via antiqua (Thomist realism)

The God who gave us Scripture also gave us minds. Creation bears the marks of its Maker, so reason can know that God exists and grasp the natural law, even though the Trinity and incarnation exceed it. Faith and reason cannot contradict each other; philosophy rightly used is the handmaid of theology, and grace does not destroy nature but perfects it.
Romans 1:20: God’s invisible attributes are clearly seen through creation
Unity of truth: God is author of both reason and revelation
Natural law makes public moral reasoning possible
Reason is darkened by sin
Aristotle’s categories may distort the gospel
Univocity and nominalist logic undermine analogy
Romans 1:19-20
Wisdom 13:1-5
Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I q.2
Via moderna (nominalism) and its Reformation heirs

God is free and not bound by our philosophical necessities. What he does, he does by his own will and promise. Reason can analyse terms and arguments, but it cannot demonstrate the deep things of God; we know them by revelation. Honesty about reason’s limits honours God’s sovereignty and protects faith from depending on Aristotle.
God’s absolute power is limited only by contradiction
Many articles of faith are indemonstrable
Economy of explanation (the razor)
Leads to fideism or voluntarism
Covenant of "doing what is in one" sounds semi-Pelagian
Weakens the knowability of natures and morality
1 Corinthians 1:18-25
Psalm 115:3
Ockham, Quodlibeta
Enlightenment rationalism

If reason is God’s gift, it must judge every claim to revelation. Whatever in religion is contrary to reason cannot be from God, and the core of true religion is what every rational person can know: God, virtue and immortality.
Universality of reason
Religious wars show the danger of unverifiable dogma
Reason itself is historically situated and fallen
Butler and Hume showed natural religion is no easier to prove

Aquinas begins the Summa Theologiae.
Paris condemnations stress God’s absolute freedom.
Ockham summoned to Avignon to answer charges about his teaching.
Luther’s Disputation against Scholastic Theology attacks Biel and Aristotle.
Toland’s Christianity not Mysterious opens the Deist controversy.
Vatican I teaches that God can be known with certainty by the natural light of reason (Dei Filius).
Aeterni Patris makes Thomism normative for Catholic schools.

Catholic teaching (Vatican I, Fides et Ratio) affirms reason’s capacity to know God while giving Aquinas special honour. Protestant traditions range from Reformed and Lutheran scholastic use of natural theology to Barthian rejection of it; Orthodox theology stresses apophatic and experiential knowledge. The question remains open across traditions.
Shaped the theological background of the Reformation.
Defined Catholic seminary education from 1879 to the 1960s.
Continues in debates over natural theology, intelligent design and public reason.
controversies/liberal-vs-dialectical-the: Does theology begin from human religious experience and history, or from God’s self-revelation alone?
Liberal versus neo-orthodox (dialectical) theology

Liberal Protestantism, from Schleiermacher to Harnack, rebuilt theology on religious experience, historical study and ethics. After 1914 Karl Barth and the dialectical theologians rejected this as making God a projection of human culture, insisting that God is known only in his self-revelation in Jesus Christ. Their public exchange in 1923 and the Church struggle in Nazi Germany made the dispute a defining one for 20th-century Protestantism.
Liberal Protestantism

Faith must be honest. Modern people cannot simply repeat ancient creeds or treat the Bible as an oracle; historical study shows how doctrines grew. Yet the essence of Christianity shines through: the God-consciousness of Jesus, the fatherhood of God, the infinite worth of the soul and the Kingdom of love. Theology must speak to educated culture and be accountable to reason and history, or it becomes arbitrary.
Intellectual honesty and historical criticism
Religious experience as universal human reality
Ethical fruit of the Kingdom of God
Collapse of liberal culture in 1914
Reduces God to human feeling or culture
Schleiermacher, On Religion (1799); The Christian Faith (1821-22)
Harnack, What Is Christianity? (1900)
Dialectical theology (neo-orthodoxy)

God is not the highest point of human religion but the wholly other who speaks. When the leading liberal theologians signed the 1914 manifesto supporting the Kaiser’s war, it became clear that a theology built on culture would bless culture. Theology’s only ground is the Word of God, Jesus Christ, attested in Scripture and proclaimed in the Church; historical study serves but cannot judge it.
Infinite qualitative difference between God and humanity (Kierkegaard)
Revelation is God’s free act, not a human possession
Barmen 1934 showed its power to resist idolatry
Risk of fideism and isolation from other disciplines
Ambiguity about Scripture’s inspiration and history
Barth, The Epistle to the Romans (1919, 1922)
Barmen Declaration (1934)
Schleiermacher’s Speeches on Religion.
Ritschl completes Justification and Reconciliation.

Barmen Declaration of the Confessing Church.

Dialectical theology dominated mid-century Protestant academies, but liberal, existentialist, process and revisionist theologies continued, and evangelicals criticised both. Many later theologians (postliberals, Moltmann, Pannenberg) sought paths beyond the opposition.
Shaped the Confessing Church and the ecumenical movement.
Divided American Protestantism between liberal, neo-orthodox and evangelical options.
Influenced postliberal theology.
controversies/homoousios-controversy/que: Is the Son homoousios (of one essence) with the Father — or the first and greatest of God's creatures?
controversies/homoousios-controversy/sum: From c. 318 to 381, the eastern Roman Empire argued over whether the Son of God is eternal and of the Father's own essence, or a creature made before time. Councils, emperors and exiles shaped the debate; the Nicene answer prevailed at Constantinople (381), while Homoian Christianity endured among the Germanic peoples for two more centuries.
controversies/homoousios-controversy/sid: We worship Christ, we are baptised into his name, and we are saved by him. If he were a creature, our worship would be idolatry and our salvation a fiction — for no creature can join creatures to God. Scripture calls him the Word who was God, through whom all things were made: he cannot be one of the things made. ‘Of one essence’ is not a philosophical novelty; it is the only phrase our opponents could not twist to their meaning.
Christians already worshipped Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11; John 20:28; Pliny's letter of c. 112).
Only God can deify: ‘He was made man that we might be made God.’
If the Father was ever without the Son, God changed — and God is unchangeable.
All things were made through the Word (John 1:3); he therefore cannot be made.
Homoousios is unbiblical and was previously condemned at Antioch (268).
It confuses the persons (Sabellianism) or implies a material substance divided between Father and Son.

We confess the Son as God's firstborn, the mighty agent of creation, worthy of honour beyond every creature. But God alone is unbegotten and without beginning. To say the Son shares the Father's very essence is either to make two unbegotten gods or to collapse the Son into the Father. Scripture says the Father is greater, that the Son learned obedience and did not know the hour. We keep to the words of Scripture; it is the Nicenes who have imported the language of the philosophers.
‘Begotten’ implies a beginning; a Son co-eternal with his Father is incoherent.
The Son confesses the Father ‘greater’ and ‘the only true God’ (John 14:28; 17:3).
Proverbs 8:22 (LXX): Wisdom says ‘the Lord created me’.
Non-scriptural terms such as ousia should not be imposed as tests of faith (Homoian creed of 359–360).
Worship of a creature is idolatry.
Divine generation is not like human generation in time; the Father is eternally Father.

We reject Arius' creature-Son as firmly as anyone: the Son is truly from the Father, Son by nature. But ‘same essence’ sounds like Sabellius and Paul of Samosata. Say rather that he is ‘like in essence’ — truly the Father's image, never confused with him.
It avoids both Arian creaturehood and Sabellian confusion.
The Son is ‘the image of the invisible God’ — an image is like, not identical to, its original.
Likeness applies to qualities, not essences; something merely like God is not God.
controversies/homoousios-controversy/tim: Arius disputes with Bishop Alexander of Alexandria; he is excommunicated by an Egyptian synod (c. 321).
Council of Nicaea adopts homoousios; Arius exiled.
Athanasius exiled to Trier by the Council of Tyre — the first of five exiles.
Arius dies in Constantinople on the eve of his readmission.
‘Blasphemy of Sirmium’ forbids ousia language; radical Anomoeanism (Aetius, Eunomius) rises.
Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia impose the Homoian creed under Constantius II.
Council of Alexandria: Athanasius reconciles with those who mean the same by different terms.
Edict of Thessalonica (Theodosius I) makes Nicene faith the religion of the empire.
Council of Constantinople reaffirms Nicaea and confesses the Spirit's deity.
Visigothic Spain abandons Homoian Christianity at Toledo III.
controversies/homoousios-controversy/res: Resolved for the imperial church at Constantinople (381) in favour of homoousios, after the Homoiousians were reconciled to Nicaea. Homoian (‘Arian’) churches persisted among Goths, Vandals and Lombards until the late 6th–7th centuries. Today nearly all churches confess the Nicene Creed; Jehovah's Witnesses and some Unitarians hold views structurally similar to Arius'.
controversies/homoousios-controversy/con: The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed became the shared creed of almost all Christians.
Established the pattern of ecumenical councils and imperial involvement in doctrine.
Created a religious divide between Nicene Romans and Homoian Germanic rulers in the post-Roman West.
Gave the Christian vocabulary of ousia and hypostasis, later needed for Christology.
